clauses.reason: The operative lead of Executive Order 6382 reads: "do order that the said code of fair competition be and it is hereby approved". It approves the Code of Fair Competition for the Rock Crusher Manufacturing Industry and states no period, condition, until-date, provisional approval or other own-terms end. The approval was code-dependent: under section 3(b) of the Act the approved provisions became the standards of fair competition for the trade or industry, under section 3(c) the district courts could restrain violations, and under section 3(f) a violation was a misdemeanor, so the approval operated only through section 3. Section 2 of S.J. Res. 113, approved June 14, 1935, provides "All the provisions of Title I of such Act delegating power to the President to approve or prescribe codes of fair competition and providing for the enforcement of such codes are hereby repealed". The resolution states no effective date other than its approval, so the approval ceased to operate on June 14, 1935. No held record shows this code cancelled or suspended before June 14, 1935. June 16, 1935 is not an end date: section 1 of the same resolution replaced the original two-year expiry of Title I with April 1, 1936, and nothing in the resolution defers section 2. Schechter (May 27, 1935) is recorded as a validity characterization, not as an end date.

research_rationale:
Executive Order 6382 (November 1, 1933) approves the Code of Fair Competition for the Rock Crusher Manufacturing Industry under Title I of the National Industrial Recovery Act. The held text is the American Presidency Project transcription (grade mirror_transcription, acceptable_as_original false; Common Crawl capture 2025-05-18T13:40:42Z); the standing note applies: original not yet held; replace and re-check quotes when an official copy is retrieved.  Because each command is dependent on the code and no held record shows an earlier end, the first end is the statutory repeal of the code approval and enforcement provisions by section 2 of S.J. Res. 113, effective June 14, 1935. Schechter, decided May 27, 1935, held the section 3 delegation unconstitutional; that is recorded as a validity characterization (void from issuance under then-prevailing doctrine), not as an end date, because the judgment cancelled no approval. The antitrust-exemption proviso of the resolution is not settled by the held text for past action; whatever survives is an accrued effect, not continued operation of the approval.

savings.reason: Acts done and liabilities incurred under the approved code before June 14, 1935 are accrued effects of the repealed approval, and the section 5 antitrust exemption for completed action taken while the approval was in effect is likewise an accrued effect; it is preserved only for past action, and nothing in S.J. Res. 113 or in any held source continues the approval or its enforcement after June 14, 1935. No held source shows a prosecution or injunction continued under this approval after that date.

source_notes.reason: The opinion of the Court states: "We think that the code-making authority thus conferred is an unconstitutional delegation of legislative power." The holding reaches section 3 approvals generally and is recorded as validity context only.
